# Runtime evidence snapshot

Generated from `evidence/claims.yaml`. Every claim was checked on its `accessed` date by the building agent. **No claim has been reviewed by a clinician.** Use these claims only within the scope stated. Say when the snapshot may be out of date. Never quote an effect size from an abstract-only claim.

## Verified against the source

You may state these, with the source link.

### CLM-BD-DEFINITION

In a 2024 survey study, neurodivergent community members roughly defined body doubling as using the presence of others to start, stay focused on, or accomplish a task; the other person can be in the same room or remote, live or recorded, known or a stranger, and need not be doing the same task.

- Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf) (Abstract; Section 4.1 'What Is Body Doubling?' (pp. 16:12-16:13))
- Does not establish: Effectiveness; a clinical or diagnostic definition.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-SURVEY

In one self-selected online survey of 220 adults (most identifying as neurodivergent, ADHD the most common self-identification, no diagnosis required), 186 said they were somewhat more likely or more likely to finish tasks when another person was present, and 108 said more likely. This is self-report with no comparison condition.

- Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf) (Section 4.3 'Use Cases' and Fig. 7 (p. 16:14); Sections 3.2-3.4 for sample)
- Does not establish: That body doubling causally improves task completion; that it helps people with clinically diagnosed ADHD; prevalence or effect size in the general ADHD population.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-VARIATION

Body doubling is not one-size-fits-all: survey respondents reported it varies by person, task, mood and availability, and some found another person's presence more distracting, a source of judgement fears or guilt-driven accountability (four respondents), or hard to arrange with a partner who was not 'too chatty'; the authors note high-accountability formats can feel stressful or overwhelming.

- Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf) (Section 4.4.3 (p. 16:17); Section 4.5.1 (pp. 16:17-16:18); Section 5 Discussion (p. 16:19))
- Does not establish: Frequency of harms; that any format is harmful.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-MODEL

Eagle et al. propose (as a descriptive model, not a tested one) that body doubling varies along two continua: space/time (from live and co-located to pre-recorded and elsewhere) and mutuality (from an aware partner you are accountable to, to ambient companionship from people unaware of their role).

- Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf) (Section 5.3 'Mapping Body Doubling' and Fig. 9 (pp. 16:21-16:22))
- Does not establish: That any region of the model is more effective.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-VR

In a non-peer-reviewed VR preprint (12 ASRS-screened adults, 20-minute bricklaying task), working with a human avatar or an 'AI' avatar both produced more bricks per minute (10.82 and 11.06) than working alone (8.49), with no difference between the two; the 'AI' double was secretly operated by a human (Wizard-of-Oz), so this does not test an autonomous AI.

- Source: [You Are Not Alone: Designing Body Doubling for ADHD in Virtual Reality](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.12153v1) (Section 5.2 (Wizard-of-Oz); Section 6.1.1-6.1.2 (sample, ASRS); Section 6.2.1 (efficiency); Section 7.2 (limitations))
- Does not establish: Effects of a real autonomous AI; long-term or real-world benefit; effects in clinically diagnosed ADHD; accuracy gains (behavioural accuracy and object detection were not significant).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-ROBOT

In a three-week in-dorm study of 11 college students with self-reported ADHD symptoms, 10 of 11 chose to keep using a small companion robot when use was voluntary, and usability was rated high (mean SUS 83.86); the robot only made pre-programmed idle motions at random times and did not respond to the student, and no objective task-performance outcome was measured.

- Source: [Design and Evaluation of a Socially Assistive Robot Schoolwork Companion for College Students with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.06289v1) (Abstract; Section 3.3 (robot behaviour); Section 3.4 (design, participants); Section 4.1 (10 of 11, SUS); Section 5.1 (limitations))
- Does not establish: Efficacy for schoolwork or ADHD symptoms (ESQ-R, NASA-TLX showed no significant change); effects of an AI or attention-monitoring system.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-MECHANISM

No source reviewed here tested or established a neurochemical (for example dopamine) mechanism for body doubling. The research papers either do not mention dopamine or list other untested theories (mirror neurons, Hawthorne effect, social facilitation, accountability); consumer pages that mention dopamine or neurotransmitters present it as speculation, an inference from general social-behaviour research, or a claim attributed to a commercial service.

- Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf); [A Roadmap of Mixed Reality Body Doubling for Adults with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.07851v1); [The ADHD Body Double: A Unique Tool for Getting Things Done](https://add.org/the-body-double/); [Could a Body Double Help You Increase Your Productivity?](https://chadd.org/adhd-weekly/could-a-body-double-help-you-increase-your-productivity/); [ADHD Body Doubling: What It Is and How It Works](https://www.psychcentral.com/adhd/adhd-body-doubling); [What Is 'Body Doubling' and Can It Help With ADHD?](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/body-doubling-for-adhd) (SRC-BD-01 Section 2 (theories); SRC-BD-05 full text (no dopamine); SRC-BD-10 (Focusmate attribution); SRC-BD-11 (dopamine inference from Kopec et al. 2019 review))
- Does not establish: That no such mechanism exists, or that no study anywhere has tested one - the search was targeted, not systematic.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-EARLY

Research on body doubling is limited and early: a 2026 work-in-progress roadmap describes it as 'a fairly new and under-researched topic', and ADHD organisations ADDA and CHADD both state that research proving its effectiveness is lacking.

- Source: [A Roadmap of Mixed Reality Body Doubling for Adults with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.07851v1); [The ADHD Body Double: A Unique Tool for Getting Things Done](https://add.org/the-body-double/); [Could a Body Double Help You Increase Your Productivity?](https://chadd.org/adhd-weekly/could-a-body-double-help-you-increase-your-productivity/) (SRC-BD-05 Introduction/Conclusion; SRC-BD-09 body text; SRC-BD-10 body text)
- Does not establish: That it is ineffective.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-NO-AI

None of the studies reviewed here evaluated an autonomous AI body double: the VR 'AI' was human-operated (Wizard-of-Oz), the robot used random pre-programmed motions, and the roadmap reports no new data.

- Source: [You Are Not Alone: Designing Body Doubling for ADHD in Virtual Reality](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.12153v1); [A Roadmap of Mixed Reality Body Doubling for Adults with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.07851v1); [Design and Evaluation of a Socially Assistive Robot Schoolwork Companion for College Students with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.06289v1) (SRC-BD-04 Section 5.2; SRC-BD-06 Section 3.3; SRC-BD-05 full text)
- Does not establish: That AI body doubling is ineffective or harmful.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-PRACTICE

ADDA runs regular 90-minute Zoom body-doubling sessions where cameras and talking are optional; this shows the practice is offered by an ADHD organisation, not that it is proven effective.

- Source: [Join Body Doubling](https://add.org/body-doubling/) (add.org/body-doubling/ session list)
- Does not establish: Effectiveness; that sessions are open to non-members; current schedule beyond access date.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-NHS-DIAGNOSIS

In the UK, ADHD should only be diagnosed by a specialist (e.g. psychiatrist or other appropriately qualified healthcare professional) after a full clinical and psychosocial assessment; a GP may refer to an ADHD specialist.

- Source: [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87); [ADHD in adults](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/) (NICE NG87 rec 1.3.1 [2008]; NHS 'Getting help with ADHD' and 'What happens at an ADHD assessment')
- Does not establish: Assessment pathways, waiting times or eligibility outside England/UK; anything about the accuracy of any specific screening tool.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-NICE-ENV

NICE describes environmental modifications as changes to the environment, tailored to an assessment of the person's needs, such as changes to seating, lighting and noise, reducing distractions (e.g. headphones), shorter periods of focus with movement breaks, and reinforcing verbal requests with written instructions.

- Source: [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87) (NICE NG87 Recommendations, 'Terms used in this guideline: Environmental modifications'; referenced in recs 1.4.3, 1.4.12, 1.5.13, 1.5.15)
- Does not establish: Effectiveness of any specific modification or of AI-delivered suggestions; that these replace clinical care (rec 1.5.15 positions them before medication review in adults, within a clinical pathway).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-NICE-SDM

NICE recommends a holistic shared treatment plan and regularly discussing with people with ADHD how they want to be involved in treatment decisions, including benefits and harms of non-drug and drug treatments and their preferences.

- Source: [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87) (NICE NG87 recs 1.5.2, 1.5.3, 1.5.4 [2018])
- Does not establish: Any role for AI in shared decision-making.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-MED-ROUTE

In the UK, ADHD medicines are started and monitored by an ADHD specialist; questions about how to take a medicine or remember doses can go to a pharmacist, and stopping should be discussed with the doctor first.

- Source: [ADHD in adults](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/); [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87); [How and when to take methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/how-and-when-to-take-methylphenidate-for-adults/) (NHS ADHD adults 'Medicines'; NICE NG87 rec 1.7.2; NHS methylphenidate 'How and when to take' (stopping, help remembering))
- Does not establish: Prescribing arrangements outside the UK; advice for any specific medicine other than as stated.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-MPH-MISSED

For methylphenidate (adults), NHS advice for a forgotten dose is to skip it and take the next dose at the usual time, and not to take 2 doses to make up for it; an alarm or a pharmacist can help with remembering.

- Source: [How and when to take methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/how-and-when-to-take-methylphenidate-for-adults/) (NHS methylphenidate for adults, 'How and when to take' > 'If you forget to take it')
- Does not establish: Missed-dose advice for any other ADHD medicine, formulation-specific or individual instructions, or non-UK advice.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-MPH-OVERDOSE

For methylphenidate (adults), the NHS advises getting urgent medical advice after taking more than prescribed even without symptoms, and emergency help for a fit or seizure or a fast, slow or irregular heartbeat.

- Source: [How and when to take methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/how-and-when-to-take-methylphenidate-for-adults/) (NHS methylphenidate for adults, 'How and when to take' > 'If you take too much')
- Does not establish: Overdose thresholds; routing outside the UK.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-MPH-URGENT

For methylphenidate (adults), the NHS lists serious side effects that need urgent medical advice (e.g. mood changes, palpitations, hallucinations, new facial tics) and ones that need emergency help (e.g. chest pain, stroke symptoms, fits, thoughts of harming yourself or others, a serious allergic reaction).

- Source: [Side effects of methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/side-effects-of-methylphenidate-for-adults/) (NHS 'Side effects of methylphenidate for adults' > 'Serious side effects' and 'Serious allergic reaction')
- Does not establish: Side-effect frequencies beyond 'uncommon (<1 in 100)'; triage by the tool; non-UK routing.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-NHS-MANAGE

NHS lists ways to manage adult ADHD including lifestyle changes, work/study adjustments, medicines and talking therapies such as CBT or mindfulness.

- Source: [ADHD in adults](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/) (NHS ADHD in adults 'How to manage ADHD')
- Does not establish: Which option suits any individual; effectiveness of self-help delivered by an AI tool.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-CADDRA-SCAFFOLD

CADDRA's guideline lists practical external supports such as structure and routines, visual reminders, timers/apps for deadlines, chunking larger tasks into smaller steps with deadlines, and planned movement breaks during prolonged tasks.

- Source: [Canadian ADHD Practice Guidelines, 4.1 Edition](https://adhdlearn.caddra.ca/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Canadian-ADHD-Practice-Guidelines-4.1-January-6-2021.pdf) (CADDRA 4.1 Edition, Chapter 4, Table 4.2 Home Interventions (printed pp. 46-47))
- Does not establish: Effectiveness of these strategies when delivered by AI; that they are treatment.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-MHRA-SAMD

MHRA guidance states a digital mental health technology is regulated as software as a medical device if it is intended to have a medical purpose and its functionality is considered complex; intended purpose is set by the manufacturer.

- Source: [Digital mental health technology: qualification and classification](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/digital-mental-health-technology-qualification-and-classification) (GOV.UK DMHT qualification and classification landing page (summary); full PDF not read)
- Does not establish: That the plugin is or is not a medical device; classification details from the 54-page PDF.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-ICO-SPECIAL

Under UK GDPR, data concerning health (including mental health) is special category data, and inferences about health can be special category data where processing aims to infer it or treats people differently on that basis.

- Source: [What is special category data?](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/lawful-basis/special-category-data/what-is-special-category-data/) (ICO 'What is special category data?' > health data; inferences)
- Does not establish: Final post-Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 position; lawful basis for this product.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-WHO-AUTONOMY

WHO's first of six principles for AI in health is protecting human autonomy: humans should remain in control of health-care systems and medical decisions, with privacy, confidentiality and informed consent protected.

- Source: [Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: WHO guidance](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240029200) (WHO news release 28 June 2021 (six guiding principles); publication page 9789240029200)
- Does not establish: Binding legal obligations; specific implementation requirements (full report not read).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-W3C-STEPS

W3C cognitive accessibility guidance recommends making each step clear: show where the user is, completed steps, the current step and pending steps, and avoid hiding completed steps or choices.

- Source: [Make Each Step Clear (Cognitive Accessibility Design Pattern)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG2/supplemental/patterns/o1p04-clear-steps/) (W3C WAI 'Make Each Step Clear', Objective 1 (Help users understand what things are and how to use them))
- Does not establish: ADHD-specific benefit; WCAG conformance requirement (supplemental only).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-DIGITAL-REVIEW

A 2026 scoping review of 133 studies of digital health technologies for adults with ADHD (Schofield et al., Frontiers in Digital Health) found the field is mostly early-stage, with frequent lack of blinding, low or unreported adherence, heavy self-report, and unclear routes into clinical practice. It did not specifically assess large language models, and it is not evidence for this software.

- Source: [Digital health technologies for adults with ADHD: a scoping review](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/digital-health/articles/10.3389/fdgth.2026.1746732/full) (Abstract, Results and Discussion (Frontiers full text, partially read))
- Does not establish: That digital tools are ineffective; anything about LLM-based assistants specifically.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-LIVED

A 2022 rapid review of 35 qualitative studies (Ginapp et al.) reported that adults with ADHD describe using regular schedules, to-do lists and reminder apps, and being helped by partners, friends, family and workplace reminders. These are self-reported coping strategies, not evidence that they work or that this software helps.

- Source: [The lived experiences of adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A rapid review of qualitative evidence](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2022.949321/full) (Results, 'Adapting to symptoms' (Coping skills; Outside support))
- Does not establish: Efficacy of any strategy; generalisability (mostly male, English-language, Europe/North America/Asia samples).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-MPH-COMMON

For methylphenidate in adults, the NHS lists common side effects (more than 1 in 100 people) as headaches, trouble sleeping, loss of appetite (with possible weight loss in the first few months), stomach ache, dry mouth and feeling or being sick, and advises telling a doctor if they bother you or don't go away.

- Source: [Side effects of methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/side-effects-of-methylphenidate-for-adults/) (NHS 'Side effects of methylphenidate for adults' > 'Common side effects of methylphenidate')
- Does not establish: Individual risk, other ADHD medicines, other formulations or other countries' labelling.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

## Checked against an abstract or summary only

State these only with a hedge, e.g. "a study summary reports…". Do not quote numbers.

### CLM-BD-EEG

A small 2025 ASSETS study (N=26; neurotypical, medicated ADHD and unmedicated ADHD participants) found no statistically significant differences between body-doubling and solo conditions on ACT reading comprehension or EEG-derived focus and calmness metrics; the authors report no consistent negative impacts and 'promising trends' for unmedicated ADHD participants.

- Source: [Reading Between the Lines: Exploring Body Doubling in ADHD Using EEG](https://doi.org/10.1145/3663547.3759743); [Evaluating the Efficacy of Body Doubling for ADHD Using a Brain-Computer Interface](https://www.ccsc.org/centralplains/2025/talks/talk-poster16/) (SRC-BD-02 abstract (via OpenAlex); SRC-BD-03 poster abstract)
- Does not establish: That body doubling does not work (underpowered null); effects on task initiation or completion; what the body double was instructed to do.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-BD-SOCIALFAC

In general (non-ADHD) research, a 1983 meta-analysis of 241 studies with nearly 24,000 participants found the mere presence of others had small effects: it sped up simple tasks and slowed complex ones, impaired accuracy on complex tasks and only slightly improved accuracy on simple tasks (a finding vulnerable to unpublished null results).

- Source: [Social facilitation: A meta-analysis of 241 studies](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.94.2.265) (Abstract)
- Does not establish: Anything specific to ADHD, body doubling or AI presence; effects on task initiation.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-GD-AADPA-CBT

The Australian guideline text indicates cognitive-behavioural interventions should be offered to adults with ADHD as an option to consider, ideally ADHD-specific and strengths-based.

- Source: [Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD: Cognitive-behavioural interventions (section 4.2.2)](https://adhdguideline.aadpa.com.au/non-pharmacological/cognitive-behavioural-interventions/cognitive-behaviour-interventions/) (AADPA guideline 4.2.2 Cognitive-behavioural interventions, evidence-to-recommendation text (adults))
- Does not establish: Formal recommendation number/grade (not captured); that AI coaching is CBT or equivalent.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-SOLANTO

In one randomised trial of 88 adults with ADHD (Solanto et al., 2010), a 12-week group meta-cognitive therapy targeting time management, organisation and planning reduced ADHD symptoms more than supportive psychotherapy. This is clinician-delivered group therapy evidence, not evidence that this software works.

- Source: [Efficacy of meta-cognitive therapy for adult ADHD](https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2009.09081123) (Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 20231319))
- Does not establish: That AI-delivered prompts, self-guided use, or this plugin replicate the effect; long-term durability; effects outside group therapy.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-SAFREN

One randomised trial of 86 medication-treated adults with persistent ADHD symptoms (Safren et al., 2010) found 12 sessions of CBT reduced symptoms more than relaxation with educational support, with gains maintained at 12 months. This concerns therapist-delivered CBT, not this software.

- Source: [Cognitive behavioral therapy vs relaxation with educational support for medication-treated adults with ADHD and persistent symptoms: a randomized controlled trial](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1192) (Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 20736471))
- Does not establish: Benefit for unmedicated adults; effectiveness of digital or AI-delivered CBT-style prompts; safety of this plugin.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-CBT-META

A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (Liu et al., Journal of Affective Disorders) reported small-to-moderate improvements with CBT in adults with ADHD for core symptoms (SMD -0.45) and executive function (SMD -0.43), but not for quality of life or self-evaluation. This is about clinician-delivered CBT, not this software.

- Source: [A meta-analysis of the intervention effect of cognitive behavioral therapy on adult ADHD](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2025.121107) (Abstract (PMID 41483880))
- Does not establish: That any AI or self-help tool produces these effects; improvement in quality of life; long-term effects.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-CBT-FUNCTION

A 2026 meta-analysis of 70 studies with 5,152 participants (López-Pinar et al., Behaviour Research and Therapy) found CBT for adult ADHD was associated with moderate gains in global functioning (SMD 0.47 post-treatment, 0.67 at follow-up), with the strongest effects for occupational functioning. Many included studies were uncontrolled, and this is not evidence for this software.

- Source: [Cognitive behavioral therapy effects on global functioning, domain-specific functioning, and quality of life in adult ADHD: A comprehensive meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brat.2026.105026) (Abstract (PMID 41936228))
- Does not establish: Causal effects from the uncontrolled studies; effects of AI or digital self-help; durable benefits beyond short follow-up (~3 months typical).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-CBT-COMPONENTS

A component network meta-analysis of 43 trials and 3,817 participants (Matsumoto et al., 2024, BMJ Mental Health) found that CBT packages including organisational strategies were associated with higher treatment response, and problem-solving components with reduced inattention. These are associations from trial-level modelling of therapist-delivered CBT, possibly including adolescents, not evidence for this software.

- Source: [Components of cognitive-behavioural therapy for mitigating core symptoms in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2024-301303) (Abstract (PMID 39732478))
- Does not establish: Causation at the component level; adult-only effects; that organisational prompts from an AI assistant are effective.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-PM-ADHD

In a 2026 experiment with 196 adults (98 with ADHD), Stelz, Edel and Altgassen found lower everyday prospective memory in the ADHD group, and found that episodic future thinking (vividly imagining carrying out an intention) at encoding improved performance compared with standard encoding. This is lab-assigned encoding instruction over three sessions, not evidence for this software.

- Source: [The impact of process- versus outcome-focused episodic future thinking on everyday prospective memory in individuals with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)](https://doi.org/10.1037/xap0000586); [Episodic Future Thinking Improves Everyday Prospective Memory Performance in Adults With a Previous Diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder by Community Providers](https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547261416467) (SRC-RS-06 abstract (PMID 42475007); SRC-RS-07 abstract (PMID 41684048))
- Does not establish: Effect sizes (not in abstract); durability; effects when prompted by an AI tool; that a 'process' focus is better (outcome focus did best).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-DELAY

Meta-analyses find that, on average, people with ADHD choose smaller immediate rewards over larger delayed ones more than controls (Jackson & MacKillop 2016, d = 0.43; Marx et al. 2021, small-to-medium effects). This is a group-average laboratory finding, not a statement about any individual and not evidence for this software.

- Source: [Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Monetary Delay Discounting: A Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Studies](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bpsc.2016.01.007); [ADHD and the Choice of Small Immediate Over Larger Delayed Rewards: A Comparative Meta-Analysis of Performance on Simple Choice-Delay and Temporal Discounting Paradigms](https://doi.org/10.1177/1087054718772138) (Abstracts (PMID 27722208; PMID 29806533))
- Does not establish: That any particular reward or nudge design improves outcomes; individual-level prediction; adult-only effects (mixed-age samples).
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-ROUTINE-SCOPING

A 2026 scoping review of 31 studies (Almudayfir et al., Behavioral Sciences) found that research on daily routines and habits in ADHD is concentrated in paediatric populations, with limited adult research and no validated ADHD-specific routine/habit measure. Routine-support features for adults therefore rest on thin direct evidence.

- Source: [Daily Routines and Habits in Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Scoping Review](https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16061000) (Abstract (PMID 42352833))
- Does not establish: That routine features help or harm adults with ADHD; any efficacy of this software.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-TIME-PERCEPTION

A 2023 review of a decade of adult ADHD time-perception research (Mette) found few studies and mixed results for time estimation and reproduction: some studies show deficits and others no clear difference. Time-blindness should not be presented as an established universal deficit.

- Source: [Time Perception in Adult ADHD: Findings from a Decade-A Review](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20043098) (Abstract (PMID 36833791))
- Does not establish: That time-perception support features help; the size of any deficit.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-EMOTION-DYSREG

A 2020 meta-analysis (Beheshti et al., BMC Psychiatry; 13 studies, N = 2,535) found emotion dysregulation was markedly elevated on average in adults with ADHD compared with controls (g = 1.17), and correlated with ADHD symptom severity (r = 0.54). This is a group average, not a diagnosis of any user, and not evidence for this software.

- Source: [Emotion dysregulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-020-2442-7) (Abstract (PMID 32164655))
- Does not establish: That any emotion-support feature is effective or safe; causality between symptoms and dysregulation.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-INTERRUPTION

Interruption research in general (non-ADHD) participants suggests that a brief warning before an interruption, which gives time to prepare, is associated with faster resumption (Trafton et al., 2003). Memory-for-goals theory (Altmann & Trafton, 2002) holds that suspended goals decay and are retrieved through cues. This is adjacent cognitive evidence. It has not been tested in ADHD or with this software.

- Source: [Preparing to resume an interrupted task: effects of prospective goal encoding and retrospective rehearsal](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1071-5819(03)00023-5); [Memory for goals: an activation-based model](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog2601_2) (SRC-RS-14 abstract snippets via web search only; SRC-RS-15 abstract (OpenAlex/PhilPapers))
- Does not establish: Effects in ADHD; effect sizes; that an AI-prompted resumption note reduces resumption cost.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-DIGITAL-RCTS

Two RCTs of self-guided or unguided digital programmes for adults with ADHD reported benefits: Kenter et al. (2023; n=120) for symptoms and quality of life vs online psychoeducation, and Baumeister et al. (2026; n=307) for quality of life when an unguided app was added to usual care, with low adherence. These were structured programmes, not this AI software.

- Source: [A self-guided internet-delivered intervention for adults with ADHD: results from a randomized controlled trial](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.invent.2023.100614); [Efficacy of an Unguided Digital Intervention for Adults With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial](https://doi.org/10.3238/arztebl.m2026.0065) (Abstracts (PMID 36969389; PMID 42240305))
- Does not establish: Efficacy of LLM/AI assistants; symptom effects in the 2026 trial (primary outcome QoL); long-term effects.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

### CLM-RS-IMPL-INTENTIONS

In general-population research, forming if-then plans (implementation intentions) had a medium-to-large average effect on goal attainment across 94 tests (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006, d = .65). This is adjacent evidence for cue-action pairing. It is not ADHD-specific and not evidence for this software.

- Source: [Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-analysis of Effects and Processes](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1) (Abstract (Semantic Scholar record))
- Does not establish: Effect in ADHD; effect when an AI suggests the plan; durability.
- Accessed: 2026-10-19

## Excluded

These claims are not asserted at runtime: CLM-GD-NHS-ONLINE-TEST.
